Visualization transforms data into a graphical representation, often with interaction, for exploration, confirmation, or presentation. Insight means recognizing a meaningful structure, trend, cluster, outlier, or relationship that supports further questions or action.
Explore customer clusters in a scatterplot.
Does the evidence support a hypothesis?
Compare score distributions in two classes.
Why use both statistics and charts

Datasets can have similar means, variances, and correlations but very different shapes: curves, outliers, or clusters. Anscombe’s quartet illustrates why summary statistics alone are insufficient. A visualization does not by itself establish causation.
The roles of people and computers

Computers calculate, filter, and render large datasets precisely. People recognize patterns, interpret them using contextual knowledge, and decide which question to ask next. Design must account for limits in attention, memory, and visual comparison.
When a number or automation may be enough

A well defined question requiring one value, such as the total number of students, may be answered directly with a number. When responses must be immediate and frequent, automated processing may be appropriate; visualization can still support monitoring and checking.

Data types in visualization describe meaning and valid comparisons. They differ from programming types such as string, int, and float. Jersey numbers 10 and 20 are labels; the player wearing 20 does not have twice the value of the player wearing 10.
Major, country, group ID, seat ID. A numeric label can still be nominal.
Poor, average, good; rank A B C. Equal spacing is not assumed.
Celsius temperature and calendar years. Zero is conventional, so ratios of values are not directly meaningful.
Mass, length, case counts, age, and race duration. Zero represents absence of the measured quantity.

GPA is quantitative: order and score differences can be discussed. In this context, GPA 80 does not mean twice the ability of GPA 40. If a measurement scale is required, state an interval-like interpretation of scores.
A seat number is nominal when it is only an identifier. The row and column obtained from a seating plan represent spatial position, not a numerical score for the seat.
A 1 to 5 star rating is usually ordinal. Any assumption of equal spacing should be stated when calculating an average.
Calendar dates are temporal and interval when considering elapsed differences. An elapsed duration is ratio. Time of day also has a cyclic structure.

An identifier is not a magnitude

A set is unordered and contains unique elements; a list is ordered and may contain duplicates; a cluster groups similar items. Sequential data progresses from low to high. Diverging data has a meaningful central reference, such as deviation from zero. Cyclic data wraps around, as hours of the day do.

Semantics guides design: the number 20 could be a temperature, a count of people, or a room ID. Each meaning implies different scales and channels. Metadata should describe units, time, definitions, and collection methods.

A mark with one distinctive feature, such as hue or orientation, can be detected rapidly before focused attention. An orange dot among gray dots is an example. A red circle among blue circles and red squares has no unique single feature; finding this conjunction target generally requires a slower search.

Perception receives and interprets sensory signals. Cognition applies knowledge to reasoning, problem solving, and decisions. Experience, expectations, and goals influence perception. The eye does not record the whole scene like a camera: vision involves fixations and saccades.

Exam answer model: Change blindness is difficulty detecting changes across separate views. For example, a point changes after a blank frame. Therefore, I would show the states side by side and highlight the changed point.

Original illustration of four visual grouping mechanisms.
Nearby elements are perceived as a group. Use spacing to separate bar groups or panels.
Elements sharing color or shape are perceived as related. Use consistent hue for the same major.
A line creates a direct relationship. Use connections to show network links.
Elements inside the same boundary are perceived as a group. Enclose a meaningful cluster.
The eye tends to follow a continuous path. This supports line chart reading; avoid confusing crossings.
The eye completes incomplete contours. Closure is distinct from grouping items inside a closed region.
Symmetry supports recognition; contrast separates a subject from its background. Keep backgrounds quiet.

Grouping cues can conflict. Placing two majors close together while using the same color for a different grouping may imply contradictory relationships. Decide which relationship matters, then choose proximity, similarity, or connection accordingly.

A mark is a geometric element representing an item or link: point, line, area, and occasionally volume. A channel is a visual property varied according to data: position, length, area, hue, lightness, shape, or orientation. Color is a channel, not a mark.
Rectangular bars, or line marks in a simplified model.
Category to position; value to length and endpoint position.
Two quantities to x and y; group to hue or shape.
Two categorical attributes to rows and columns; value to lightness.
Items to nodes; relationships to connections.
Value to circle area, rather than linearly to radius.

An encoding should convey the information present in the data accurately. Nominal categories have no inherent order: assigning increasing sizes to major IDs can imply a false ranking. Unordered discrete hues do not clearly express the magnitude of scores.

Important attributes should use effective, noticeable channels. For quantitative comparison, prefer position on a common scale, followed by unaligned positions, length, angle, and area. Depth, luminance, and volume are generally less accurate for this task. Rankings depend on the task; they are not universal rules for every dataset.

Redundant encoding maps one attribute to multiple channels, such as major to both hue and shape. Separability concerns whether viewers can read channels independently. Avoid combinations that interfere with or conceal one another.
Study source: C4, PDF pages 3 to 15, 19 to 29, and 43 to 48.

Angles and unaligned segments are difficult to compare.

Spread, outliers, and multiple modes are hidden.
Add raw points, a boxplot, or a violin plot as appropriate.
The viewer must remember previous frames.
Use small multiples with consistent scales and ordering.

The displayed magnitude should correspond to the data magnitude. Under the usual relative change definition, the lie factor is the percentage change shown in the graphic divided by the percentage change in the data. State the baseline and how you measure each effect.

For example, 100 to 110 is a 10% increase. If bars begin at 90, visible lengths change from 10 to 20, a 100% increase. The lie factor is 10. This division is undefined when the data effect is zero. Do not mix size ratios with percentage increases.

Bar charts normally require zero because length encodes magnitude. Line charts and dotplots may use clearly labelled narrower domains to reveal variation. Increasing the data ink ratio does not mean removing useful axes, labels, or context.

A confidence interval for a mean describes uncertainty in the estimated mean, not a region containing most observations. Show the distribution or raw data to communicate distributional shape. How to Answer Chart Analysis Questions

Use a sentence with an object and a comparison: The goal is to compare methylation percentages across organs and indicators to find pairs with high values. Avoid vague statements such as to visualize the data.
State the item or unit of observation, list attributes and their types, and record units and time. When a diagram uses real positions, distinguish the identifier from the spatial position.

Use this pattern: Each ... mark represents ...; the ... channel encodes ... . For example, each circle represents a country; text gives its name and age; hue encodes an age band. The approximate geographic layout does not rank ages.

Include marks, axes, ticks, labels, units, and a legend when needed. State the new mapping, explain how it supports the task, and acknowledge a tradeoff. A ranked dotplot compares ages well but reduces geographic context; a small map can be added if location matters.

Define fixed SVG and inner plotting area.

Use scaleBand for categories on x and scaleLinear from zero to the maximum on y. SVG y coordinates increase downward, so the y range is [innerHeight, 0]. A bar starts at y(value); its height is innerHeight minus y(value); its width is x.bandwidth().

Use scaleLinear on x with domain from zero to the maximum and range [0, innerWidth]; use scaleBand on y. The bar starts at x = 0, its width is x(value), its y position is y(key), and its height is y.bandwidth().
Do not accidentally coerce null or an empty string to zero. Handle missing values according to their meaning.
Numeric sorting needs a comparator, for example (a,b) => b.Horsepower - a.Horsepower. Default string sorting can give the wrong order.
If no valid records remain, display a message and stop instead of creating a scale with an undefined domain.
